name: コンフェクション アーティザナル ブレッド&スイーツ (Confection Artisanal Bread & Sweets)

claims.text: The entire shop is a wheat-flour bakery blending many wheat varieties, so flour and gluten are pervasive throughout the space.
Pastries and croissants use French fermented butter and the range includes dairy and egg products, sharing the same prep area as any plant-based item.
Croissants are made egg-free, which can help visitors avoiding eggs.
Pasta, bread, and desserts are all handmade in-house, so wheat flour is worked throughout the small kitchen and cross-contact would be unavoidable for a celiac diner.
Menu is built around meat, seafood, cheese and animal-based Italian preparations; no separate vegan handling is documented.
Wheat somen and udon are core menu items prepared in the same kitchen, so cross-contamination with gluten is effectively unavoidable.
Creative Japanese and izakaya dishes use standard soy sauce and miso, which contain wheat; no wheat-free seasoning is documented.
Most dishes use fish dashi and the signature miso soup is made with milk, so vegan-safe preparation is not assured without asking.
Lunch sets are customizable with choices across proteins, sides and rice, so there is some flexibility to assemble a more vegetable-forward plate if you ask.

name: 絵本とコーヒーのパビリオン (Ehon to Coffee no Pavilion)

claims.text: The café bakes its own cheesecake, scones, and daily cakes on site, so wheat flour is handled in the kitchen and there is no indication of any gluten-free preparation or separation.
Signature items (custard pudding, cheesecake, café au lait) rely on dairy and eggs; no dairy-free or egg-free preparation is mentioned.
Plain self-roasted black coffee is served without milk and is naturally free of gluten and animal products.

name: french o・mo・ya 奈良町 (French o・mo・ya Naramachi (Furenchi Omoya Nar)

claims.text: Courses include bread and French sauces, and there is no gluten-free menu or celiac-safe handling described, so cross-contact with wheat is likely.
Menus center on meat and fish with French sauces typically using butter, cream and stock; no vegan or vegetarian course is published, so shared preparation with animal products is expected.
The restaurant indicates it can remove specific allergens on request when arranged in advance, with staff coordinating with the chef.
No published allergen or cross-contamination policy. Although the soba is 100% buckwheat with no wheat binder, the dipping sauce and kitchen are not gluten-free controlled.
Soba is served with traditional tsuyu, which is based on soy sauce that normally contains wheat.
Standard soba tsuyu uses fish-based dashi (katsuo), so default preparations are not vegan; no vegan accommodation is documented.
The noodles are juwari (100% buckwheat) with no wheat flour used as a binder.
Noodles are boiled individually per order rather than in a shared batch, which reduces (but does not eliminate) noodle-to-noodle cross-contact; a fully dedicated GF pot/water is unconfirmed.
The tsuyu is a kombu/shiitake/bonito dashi finished with soy sauce; standard soy sauce contains wheat, so a tamari-based dip must be requested and is unconfirmed.
Dipping dashi contains bonito; mizu-soba (water + ume) is the only plausibly plant-based option and should be confirmed.
No published gluten-free or allergen policy; celiac accommodation (tamari, dedicated water) is unverified and must be arranged directly.
Both soba types are jūwari (100% buckwheat) with no wheat binder, hand-milled fresh each morning.
Each portion is boiled to order rather than in a shared batch.
Oden items share a single simmering pot of soy-sauce-seasoned dashi, so wheat-containing broth contacts everything cooked in it.
Oden and home-style obanzai are seasoned with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.
Oden and obanzai are built on fish dashi (bonito/kombu), so even vegetable dishes are unlikely to be free of animal-derived stock.
